Oh sweet, i've heard that Utah has some great canyons and all. I might just have to take a trip there one day. Any specific trails you recommend?

I would have to find my topo map to give you specific trail names. Having said that, literally anywhere in the backcountry is breathtaking. Just make sure you sign in and get a backcountry permit so the rangers know you are out there, just in case.

The biggest challenge is finding water. Do your research and be prepared. Also, the weather can change fast. One early spring trip, we got iced in and couldn't travel for days until it melted. The trail at that point was over what's called slickrock which is exactly what it sounds like. When dry, it's great, but if covered in ice it is a game changer.

Even moving around our campsite was a nightmare just trying to stay upright.

Ahh I see, very helpful advice indeed. Where do you recommend that I get a backcountry permit? And I'm used to being able to just purify water with iodine and whatnot, any recommendations for the water situation?

You should run across a ranger station (outpost is a better description) beside the road on the way into the area. It's a tiny little shack on the right hand side of the road. You can also get water in that area or at the primitive campground. Somewhere right in that general vicinity.

As for backcountry water, it can sometimes be found in small catch basins, but must be purified or filtered. I'd also recommend boiling as well. Or even all of the above. ;)

In some areas, water is so scarce when I accidentally spilled some, small lizards darted in to lick it up! It was crazy cool. You are going to most likely, depending on what area you visit, pack in more water than you ever imagined. I carried 3 one quart nalgene bottles and we shared the load on a 5 gallon collapsible container as well for two of us. (Note it became easier day after day as we used it)

That is also problematical at times, trying to maintain footing and handholds while carrying that much water. You can find more information here.

The one thing to remember in a desert environment at all times: stay hydrated! While it is possible to find some water along the way, it's not something you can count on in certain areas.

Having said all this, the terrain varies wildly, it really depends on where you go. We visited The Needles District on our trips.
